title: The campaign was the product
lede: Almost everything written about OK is about how it was sold. The methods were unusual for a soft drink in 1994: mail, a telephone line, text on a black screen, and a brand voice that mocked the claims brands make.

blocks.title: A hotline that answered back
blocks.body:
Callers could listen to other callers, leave a message or take the “OK Personality Inventory,” a true-or-false test read in what Time called “ironic tones.” A sample statement: “Sometimes people who feel OK don’t deserve it.”[^6] The Believer traces the test to the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory and the hotline to an art project, Allan Bridge’s Apology Line.[^13]

Callers were warned that their comments “may be used in advertising or exploited in some other way we haven’t figured out yet.”[^13] They were. “Carbonated tree sap” went from a voicemail into the ads.[^8]
blocks.caption: Both of Coca-Cola’s Minneapolis focus groups kept calling the 800 number from the observation room.[^6] Original illustration.

blocks.title: Chain letters, then chain letters on television
blocks.body:
The letters went out about two weeks before the ads. They promised the usual rewards of a chain letter in the brand’s deadpan: a recipient in North Dakota who followed the instructions found within a month that he had “appeared on nationally syndicated talk shows as an unlikely sex symbol.”[^6]

The television spots then read the letters aloud over scrolling typewriter text. A follow-up spot reported complaints from a group called Americans Mad About OK, which did not exist.[^13] Wegner told The Washington Post that critics were taking it too literally: “It’s a game. We’re just playing a more sophisticated game.”[^8]
blocks.caption: Recipients could keep the chain going by mailing the letter or by showing it to six friends.[^6] Original illustration.

blocks.title: From the manifesto
blocks.subtitle: Five of the ten points, as printed in The Believer. Several appeared on the cans.
rows: What’s the point of OK? Well, what’s the point of anything?
OK Soda says, “Don’t be fooled into thinking there has to be a reason for everything.”
There is no real secret to feeling OK.
Never overestimate the remarkable abilities of “OK” brand soda.
Please wake up every morning knowing that things are going to be OK.
blocks.source: Michael Schulman, The Believer, Feb 2014.[^13] Versions of points 1 and 4 are also quoted from the cans by Time in 1994 and 1997.[^6][^10]
